questions.q: On a position-versus-time (displacement-time) graph, the gradient of the line — its rise over run — is equal to which quantity?
options: The acceleration of the object
The velocity of the object
The displacement of the object
The distance travelled by the object
questions.explanation: For Steady Sam the textbook shows the average velocity and instantaneous velocity are both equal to the gradient of the position-versus-time graph, because gradient = rise/run = change in position / time = velocity. A flat line is therefore at rest, and a steeper line is a larger velocity.

questions.q: On a curved position-versus-time graph, how do you find the instantaneous velocity at a single instant?
options: Take the area under the curve up to that instant
Read the position value straight off the vertical axis
Find the gradient of the tangent to the curve at that point
Divide the final position by the total time
questions.explanation: The textbook shows that as the time interval shrinks, the line joining two points approaches a tangent to the curve; the gradient of the tangent to the curve equals the instantaneous velocity at the instant where it meets the curve. For Beryl at 4.0 s this gradient (rise/run) gives 8.0 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: What does the area under a velocity-versus-time graph represent?
options: The acceleration during the interval
The displacement (change in position) during the interval
The average velocity during the interval
The gradient of the motion
questions.explanation: The textbook states that the area under any part of the velocity-versus-time graph is equal to the displacement during the interval represented by that part. It can be found by counting squares or by dividing the area into rectangles and triangles.

questions.q: Steady Sam runs at a constant velocity of 6.7 m s⁻¹ west for 15 s. Find his displacement using the area of the rectangle under the velocity-versus-time graph.
working: Constant velocity gives a rectangle under the velocity-versus-time graph.
questions.explanation: Because the velocity is constant, the area under the graph is a rectangle: area = length × width = 15 s × 6.7 m s⁻¹ = 100 m, which equals the displacement, matching the textbook's worked value.

questions.q: The motion of an elevator is shown on a velocity-versus-time graph. How is the acceleration at any instant determined from this graph?
options: By calculating the gradient of the graph at that instant
By taking the area under the graph at that instant
By reading the velocity value straight off the axis
By multiplying velocity by time
questions.explanation: The textbook states the acceleration at any instant during the motion can be determined by calculating the gradient of the velocity-versus-time graph, as a consequence of the definition of acceleration. Where the velocity is constant the gradient is zero, so the acceleration is zero.

questions.q: On the elevator's velocity-versus-time graph, during interval C the velocity changes by −8.0 m s⁻¹ over 2.5 s. Calculate the acceleration during interval C.
working: Acceleration is the gradient of the velocity-versus-time graph.
questions.explanation: The gradient of the velocity-versus-time graph during interval C is −8.0 m s⁻¹ ÷ 2.5 s = −3.2 m s⁻², exactly as the textbook computes. The negative sign means the acceleration is directed downward.

questions.q: Just as the area under a velocity-versus-time graph gives change in position, what does the area under an acceleration-versus-time graph equal?
options: The displacement of the object
The change in velocity of the object
The instantaneous acceleration of the object
The distance travelled by the object
questions.explanation: The textbook states that the area under an acceleration-versus-time graph is equal to the change in velocity of an object, mirroring how the area under a velocity-versus-time graph gives the change in position (displacement).

questions.q: From memory: state the three core rules of motion graphs, and the 'gradient climbs, area descends' hook that ties them together.
keyPoints: The gradient of a displacement-time graph is the velocity.
The gradient of a velocity-time graph is the acceleration.
The area under a velocity-time graph is the displacement (area below the axis is negative).
Gradient climbs the ladder (displacement to velocity to acceleration); area on a velocity-time graph descends back to displacement.
questions.explanation: If you recalled all three rules and the ladder hook, grade Good or Easy. The golden trap from the episode: on a velocity-time graph, gradient is acceleration and area is displacement — never mix the two operations.

questions.q: In your own words: a horizontal line on a displacement-time graph and a horizontal line on a velocity-time graph mean two completely different things. What does each one mean?
keyPoints: Horizontal line on a displacement-time graph: the displacement is not changing, so the object is at rest (stationary).
Horizontal line on a velocity-time graph: the velocity is not changing, so the object moves at constant velocity with zero acceleration.
The difference arises because the vertical axis represents a different quantity in each graph.
questions.explanation: This is the single most tested distinction in motion graphs. At rest versus constant velocity — the only way to tell them apart is to know which graph you are reading. If you got both, grade Good or Easy.

questions.q: A velocity-time graph shows an object whose velocity increases uniformly from zero to 20 m s⁻¹ in 5 s, then decreases uniformly back to zero over the next 10 s. Calculate the total displacement and state what the gradient of each section tells you. (4 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: The total displacement is the area under the graph. First section (0–5 s): a triangle of area ½ × 5 s × 20 m s⁻¹ = 50 m. Second section (5–15 s): a triangle of area ½ × 10 s × 20 m s⁻¹ = 100 m. Total displacement = 50 + 100 = 150 m. The gradient of the first section is 20 ÷ 5 = 4 m s⁻², a positive acceleration (speeding up). The gradient of the second section is (0 − 20) ÷ 10 = −2 m s⁻², a negative acceleration (slowing down). The displacement came from areas and both accelerations came from gradients, kept cleanly separate.

criteria.descriptor: Two triangular areas summed to 150 m total displacement.
Gradient of first section = +4 m s⁻² (positive acceleration, speeding up).
Gradient of second section = −2 m s⁻² (negative acceleration, slowing down).
Links each gradient to acceleration and the areas to displacement, keeping the two operations separate.

questions.explanation: The whole skill: area under the velocity-time graph for displacement, gradient for acceleration, never confusing the two.
